Apache

Apache is an umbrella name connecting distinct peoples, languages and sovereign governments, rather than one political nation. Community histories encompass the Southwest, southern Plains and northern Mexico. The Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, Mescalero Apache Tribe, San Carlos Apache Tribe and Yavapai-Apache Nation illustrate different histories within this broader field.

Names & relationshipsApache is a wider grouping. Plains/Kiowa Apache, Mescalero, Lipan, Chiricahua and Western Apache histories overlap without being interchangeable. The Fort Sill Apache Tribe and Apache Tribe of Oklahoma are separate governments; Yavapai is a distinct people within the Yavapai-Apache Nation.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

A broad name with distinct political meanings

The Apache Tribe of Oklahoma, also called Plains Apache, is a distinct community rather than another name for all Apache peoples. The Oklahoma Historical Society explains that its people maintain a separate linguistic and cultural identity despite long associations with Kiowa and other Plains nations. The Yavapai-Apache Nation offers another important distinction: it joins two peoples, Yavapai and Apache, in one government. Its Apache people identify as Dil’zhe’e, while its Yavapai people identify as Wipuhk’a’bah. A shared government and a broad ethnographic name therefore describe different kinds of relationships.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society [2] Yavapai-Apache Nation

02

Land use was diverse and place-specific

San Carlos Apache history describes seasonal movement between river valleys and higher country, combining hunting and plant gathering with fields of corn, squash and beans. Acorns and mescal were important foods. The Plains Apache in Oklahoma followed a different regional trajectory: the Oklahoma Historical Society describes mobile bison hunting on the Great Plains, followed by confinement to western Oklahoma reservation lands from 1867 to allotment in 1901. These different settings and histories shaped livelihoods. Accounts centered entirely on warfare miss the agricultural knowledge and varied uses of landscapes described in these sources.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society [3] San Carlos Apache Tribe

03

Confinement and exile reshaped communities

San Carlos’s history explains how settler pressure, the 1871 Camp Grant Massacre and reservation confinement restricted movement and separated children from families through assimilationist schooling. Fort Sill Apache history follows a different sequence: Chiricahua people were imprisoned in Florida and Alabama before their transfer to Oklahoma in 1894. Some later joined Mescalero; others insisted on lands they had been promised near Fort Sill and were released and resettled on allotments in 1914. Their present locations must be understood through these forced movements.

Read the sources [3] San Carlos Apache Tribe [4] Fort Sill Apache Tribe

04

Mescalero and Lipan histories cross the border

The Mescalero Apache Tribe identifies Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua as its three constituent groups. Its history dates the reservation’s establishment by executive order to May 29, 1873, with Lipan arrivals from northern Chihuahua around 1903 and Chiricahua arrivals in 1913. The Lipan Apache Tribe’s own account also follows communities that remained in Texas and moved between Texas and Mexico. Membership in Mescalero consequently does not encompass every Lipan community. The international boundary cuts across histories of refuge, dispossession, kinship and survival.

Read the sources [5] Mescalero Apache Tribe [6] Lipan Apache Tribe

05

Language and cultural transmission

The San Carlos Apache Language Preservation Program operates under tribal council direction. Its work includes Elder interviews, collecting place names and knowledge of plants and animals, teaching classes, and developing resources for families and young people. Mescalero’s cultural account places language, Elder guidance and family responsibility within continuing community life; it describes the girls’ coming-of-age ceremony as a major collective commitment. These examples belong to particular communities and should not be presented as identical practices across all Apache peoples.

Read the sources [5] Mescalero Apache Tribe [7] San Carlos Apache Tribe

06

Governments and public institutions today

Tribal websites also document contemporary government and services. The Yavapai-Apache Nation lists courts, health care, housing, youth services and educational support, and explains how economic enterprises help fund them. The Fort Sill Apache Tribe’s history records constitutional organization, land acquisition in its ancestral region and a New Mexico reservation proclamation in 2011. These institutions demonstrate continuing political life after confinement and displacement. They also provide separate starting points for studying each government’s own citizenship, laws, priorities and relationship with its homeland.
